The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{2,3\}$ and let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, bounded, connected, and Lipschitz. Use the real spaces $V=H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$ and $Q=L^2_0(D)$, norms $\|v\|_V=\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(D)}$ and $\|q\|_Q=\|q\|_{L^2(D)}$, and $b(v,q)=-\int_Dq\,\operatorname{div}v$ as in [[def-na-stokes-zero-mean-pressure-and-velocity-spaces]]. For a real normed space $X$, write $X'$ for its continuous real dual with operator norm $\|F\|_{X'}=\sup_{\|x\|_X\le1}|F(x)|$. Let $\mu\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb R)$ satisfy $0<\mu_0\le\mu(x)\le\mu_1<\infty$ almost everywhere, let $\lambda\ge0$ be a scalar, and let $f\in V'$. For any $w,z\in H^1(D;\mathbb R^d)$ define $\varepsilon(w)=(\nabla w+\nabla w^T)/2$ and
$$a_\mu(w,z)=2\int_D\mu\,\varepsilon(w):\varepsilon(z),\qquad \mathcal E_\lambda(w,z)=a_\mu(w,z)+\lambda\int_D\operatorname{div}w\,\operatorname{div}z,$$
and $\sigma_\lambda(w)=2\mu\varepsilon(w)+\lambda(\operatorname{div}w)I_d$. The homogeneous-Dirichlet model restricts these forms to $V$, with displacement zero on the full boundary; an example may prescribe a different boundary partition but gains no well-posedness claim from this definition. This is a linear small-strain model; no nonlinear, injectivity, or contrast-independent estimate is asserted.

Countable Choice is inherited through the imported Sobolev and Stokes-space conventions; this definition makes no arbitrary-index selection.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open, and suppose its first coordinate projection is contained in an interval $(a,b)$ of width $L=b-a$. For every real $v\in H^1_0(D)$,
$$\|v\|_{L^2(D)}\le L\|\partial_1v\|_{L^2(D)}\le L\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(D)}.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. On $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[def-hk-and-hk-zero-notation]]) define $$(u,v)_{H^1}:=(u,v)_{L^2}+\sum_{i=1}^n(D_iu,D_iv)_{L^2},$$ with the $L^2$ inner product of [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. Then $(\cdot,\cdot)_{H^1}$ is an inner product on the Sobolev classes whose induced norm is the $W^{1,2}$ norm of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], and $H^1(\Omega)$ is a Hilbert space for it. The zero-boundary space $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a closed subspace of $H^1(\Omega)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]) and hence a Hilbert space for the restricted inner product. The pairing is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, in the convention of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]].

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume Countable Choice. For bounded open $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ and $v\in H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$, put $\varepsilon(v)=(
abla v+
abla v^T)/2$. Then
$$2\|\varepsilon(v)\|_2^2=\|
abla v\|_2^2+\|\operatorname{div}v\|_2^2,$$
so $\|
abla v\|_2\le\sqrt2\|\varepsilon(v)\|_2$.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $V$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let
$a:V\times V\to\mathbb K$ be linear in its first argument, conjugate-linear
in its second, bounded by $M$, and coercive with constant $\alpha>0$:
$$|a(v,w)|\le M\|v\|_V\|w\|_V,\qquad \operatorname{Re}a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|_V^2.$$
Let $F:V\to\mathbb K$ be bounded and conjugate-linear, and let $V_h\subseteq V$
be finite-dimensional. Then there are unique $u\in V$ and $u_h\in V_h$ with
$$a(u,v)=F(v)\quad(v\in V).$$
$$a(u_h,v_h)=F(v_h)\quad(v_h\in V_h).$$
The solutions satisfy
$$\|u-u_h\|_V\le\frac M\alpha\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_V.$$
The real bilinear case uses linear functionals and reads $\operatorname{Re}$ as
the identity.

derivations.claim: Since $|\varepsilon(v)|_F\le|\nabla v|_F$ and $|\operatorname{div}v|\le\sqrt d|\nabla v|_F$, [F4] gives $|\mathcal E_\lambda(u,v)|\le(2\mu_1+d\lambda)\|u\|_V\|v\|_V$. The form is real, symmetric, and bounded.
By [F3] and $\mu\ge\mu_0$, $\mathcal E_\lambda(v,v)\ge2\mu_0\|\varepsilon(v)\|_2^2\ge\mu_0\|v\|_V^2$; the volumetric term is nonnegative.
By [F1]–[F2], $V$ is complete in $\|\cdot\|_V$. Applying [F5] to the bounded functional $f$ and the form of steps 1.1–1.2 yields a unique $u\in V$.

Testing with $v=u$ gives $\mathcal E_\lambda(u,u)=f(u)\le\|f\|_{V'}\|u\|_V$ and, by step 1.2, $\mu_0\|u\|_V^2\le\|f\|_{V'}\|u\|_V$. If $u\ne0$, divide by $\mu_0\|u\|_V$; if $u=0$, the claimed bound is immediate. Substitution into the energy identity gives the second estimate.

The form bounds in step 1.1 and the coercivity constant $\mu_0$ in step 1.2 satisfy the hypotheses of [F6] on every finite-dimensional conforming $V_h$. Thus its Galerkin solution is unique and the stated $M/\alpha$ estimate is exactly $M=2\mu_1+d\lambda$, $\alpha=\mu_0$.

1. $f=g$ almost everywhere;
2. for every measurable $A$,
   $$\int_A f\,d\mu=\int_A g\,d\mu.$$

$|h\chi_A|\le|h|$.

complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev

are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs

for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open, and suppose its first coordinate projection is contained in an interval $(a,b)$ of width $L=b-a$. For every real $v\in H^1_0(D)$,
$$\|v\|_{L^2(D)}\le L\|\partial_1v\|_{L^2(D)}\le L\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(D)}.$$

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open, let $0<\lambda<\infty$, and let $u\in H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$. Since $D$ has finite measure, Hölder's inequality makes every $L^2(D)$ representative integrable, and almost-everywhere equal representatives have the same integral. Thus the local mean-zero space
$$Q_D:=\left\{q\in L^2(D;\mathbb R):\int_Dq=0\right\}.$$
Set $p=-\lambda\operatorname{div}u$. Then $p\in Q_D$. If additionally $d\in\{2,3\}$ and $D$ is nonempty, connected, and Lipschitz, this $Q_D$ is exactly the space $Q=L^2_0(D)$ of [[def-na-stokes-zero-mean-pressure-and-velocity-spaces]], so $p$ belongs to the mixed elasticity model's pressure space.

derivations.claim: The pointwise bounds $|\varepsilon(v)|_F\le|\nabla v|_F$ and $|\operatorname{div}v|\le\sqrt d|\nabla v|_F$, together with [F9], give $|a_\mu(u,v)|\le2\mu_1\|u\|_V\|v\|_V$ and $|b(v,q)|\le\sqrt d\|v\|_V\|q\|_Q$. By [F3], $a_\mu(v,v)\ge2\mu_0\|\varepsilon(v)\|_2^2\ge\mu_0\|v\|_V^2$.

The space $V$ is a closed subspace of $H^1(D;\mathbb R^d)$ and its gradient norm is equivalent to the $H^1$ norm by [F8]; $Q$ is the closed kernel of the bounded integral functional on $L^2(D)$. Thus both are real Hilbert spaces under [A1]. Also $Q\ne\{0\}$: two disjoint positive-measure balls inside $D$ give a nonzero difference of indicator functions with zero integral. And $V\ne\{0\}$: choose a ball $B(x_0,r)$ with closure in $D$ and set $\phi(x)=\exp(-1/(r^2-|x-x_0|^2))$ inside it and zero outside. Its derivatives vanish at the sphere, so $\phi\in C_c^\infty(D)$ is nonzero and $(\phi,0,\ldots,0)\in V$.

For finite $\lambda>0$, take the primal solution from [F7] and set $p_\lambda=-\lambda\operatorname{div}u_\lambda$. By [F2, F10], $p_\lambda\in Q$. Then $a_\mu(u_\lambda,v)+b(v,p_\lambda)=a_\mu(u_\lambda,v)+\lambda(\operatorname{div}u_\lambda,\operatorname{div}v)=f(v)$, while $b(u_\lambda,q)-\lambda^{-1}(p_\lambda,q)=-(\operatorname{div}u_\lambda,q)+(\operatorname{div}u_\lambda,q)=0$. Conversely, any mixed solution has $s=\operatorname{div}u+\lambda^{-1}p\in Q$ by [F2]; its second equation gives $(s,q)=0$ for every $q\in Q$, hence $s=0$ by choosing $q=s$. It therefore solves the unique primal equation and has the same pressure.

At $\lambda=0$, use the primal solution and set $p_0=0$ by convention. At $\lambda=\infty$, apply [F6] to $V,Q$, $a=a_\mu$, and $b$ with $G=0$: [F1] and step 1.1 give bounded forms, step 1.1 gives coercivity on all of $V$, [F4] gives the inf-sup bound, and step 1.2 gives real Hilbert spaces with both $V,Q$ nonzero. This yields a unique mean-zero pair $(u_\infty,p_\infty)$.

For each discrete pair, [F5] supplies a positive $\beta_h$ bounded below independently of $h$. For finite $\lambda>0$ or $\lambda=\infty$, write $c=\lambda^{-1}\ge0$, with $c=0$ at infinity. A homogeneous discrete mixed solution $(w_h,r_h)$ satisfies $a_\mu(w_h,v_h)+b(v_h,r_h)=0$ and $b(w_h,q_h)-c(r_h,q_h)=0$. Test with $v_h=w_h$ and $q_h=r_h$ and subtract the second equality from the first to get $a_\mu(w_h,w_h)+c\|r_h\|_Q^2=0$. Step 1.1 forces $w_h=0$, and then discrete inf-sup forces $r_h=0$. The square finite-dimensional block matrix is injective, hence bijective, so the discrete system has a unique solution for every right-hand side.

The same stability estimate applies to any solution of $a_\mu(w,v)+b(v,r)=F(v)$, $b(w,q)-c(r,q)=G(q)$ when the inf-sup constant is $\beta>0$. Put $U=\|w\|_V$, $P=\|r\|_Q$, $F_0=\|F\|_{V'}$, and $G_0=\|G\|_{Q'}$. Testing with $v=w$ and $q=r$ and subtracting gives $\mu_0U^2\le F_0U+G_0P$. The first equation and inf-sup give $\beta P\le F_0+2\mu_1U$. With $S=F_0+G_0$ and $A=1+2\mu_1/\beta$, substitution, using $F_0G_0\le S^2/4$, yields $\mu_0U^2\le ASU+S^2/(4\beta)$. Solving this quadratic gives $U\le C_US$, where $C_U=(A+\sqrt{A^2+\mu_0/\beta})/(2\mu_0)$; then $P\le C_PS$ with $C_P=\beta^{-1}(1+2\mu_1C_U)$. Thus $U+P\le C_*S$ for $C_*=C_U+C_P$, and these constants do not depend on $c$.

For $0<\lambda\le\mu_0$, let $P_h:Q\to Q_h$ be the $L^2$-orthogonal projection. It exists uniquely: in a basis of the finite-dimensional $Q_h$, its defining normal equations have the positive-definite Gram matrix $((q_i,q_j))$, and orthogonality gives $\|p-P_hp\|_Q=\inf_{q_h\in Q_h}\|p-q_h\|_Q$. The second mixed equation gives $p_h=-\lambda P_h\operatorname{div}u_h$. Hence the first is the symmetric discrete equation $a_h(u_h,v_h)=f(v_h)$, where $a_h(w,v)=a_\mu(w,v)+\lambda(P_h\operatorname{div}w,P_h\operatorname{div}v)$. For any $w_h\in V_h$, subtract the equation for $a_h(w_h,\cdot)$ from the continuous primal equation. For every $v_h\in V_h$ this gives $a_h(u_h-w_h,v_h)=a_h(u-w_h,v_h)+\lambda((I-P_h)\operatorname{div}u,(I-P_h)\operatorname{div}v_h)$. Since $p=-\lambda\operatorname{div}u$, $\lambda(I-P_h)\operatorname{div}u=-(I-P_h)p$; orthogonal projection gives $\|I-P_h\|\le1$, while $\|\operatorname{div}v_h\|_2\le\sqrt d\|v_h\|_V$, so Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the remainder by $\sqrt d\|p-P_hp\|_Q\|v_h\|_V$. Testing with $v_h=u_h-w_h$ and using coercivity yields the displacement estimate; if $u_h=w_h$ it is immediate, and otherwise divide by $\mu_0\|u_h-w_h\|_V$ and take the infimum over $w_h$: $\|u-u_h\|_V\le\left(1+\frac{M_0}{\mu_0}\right)\inf_{w_h\in V_h}\|u-w_h\|_V+\frac{\sqrt d}{\mu_0}\inf_{q_h\in Q_h}\|p-q_h\|_Q$. For $\lambda=0$, [F7] gives the solution bounds and the displacement estimate with constant $2\mu_1/\mu_0$; $p_0=p_{h,0}=0$. Write $\|(v,q)\|_{V\times Q}=\|v\|_V+\|q\|_Q$. Let $x=(u,p)$ be the continuous solution, $x_h=(u_h,p_h)$ its Galerkin solution, and fix $y_h=(v_h,q_h)\in V_h\times Q_h$. Let $K\in\mathbb R^{N\times N}$ be symmetric positive semidefinite, let $R\in\mathbb R^{N\times r}$ have full column rank and satisfy $\ker K=\operatorname{range}R$, and let $f\in\mathbb R^N$ be compatible in the sense $R^Tf=0$. Define the gauge solve as the procedure:

1. Form the square augmented matrix and right-hand side
$$
\begin{bmatrix}K&R\\R^T&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad \begin{bmatrix}f\\0\end{bmatrix}.
$$
2. Solve for $(u,\gamma)\in\mathbb R^N\times\mathbb R^r$.
3. Return $u$, which is the representative satisfying $R^Tu=0$.

The input hypotheses must be checked for the particular stiffness matrix. The procedure does not identify an omitted nullspace or assert a load is compatible.

derivations.claim: Suppose $(x,\eta)$ lies in the nullspace of the augmented matrix. Then $Kx+R\eta=0$ and $R^Tx=0$. Multiplying the first equation by $x^T$ gives $x^TKx+x^TR\eta=0$, and the second equation makes the second term zero; hence $x^TKx=0$.

For any $y\in\mathbb R^N$ and $t\in\mathbb R$, positive semidefiniteness gives $(x+ty)^TK(x+ty)=2t y^TKx+t^2y^TKy\ge0$. If $y^TKx\ne0$, choosing $t$ with the opposite sign and sufficiently small magnitude makes the right side negative. Thus $y^TKx=0$ for every $y$, so $Kx=0$.

Since $\ker K=\operatorname{range}R$, write $x=Ra$. Then $0=R^Tx=R^TRa$; full column rank makes $R^TR$ positive definite, so $a=0$ and $x=0$. The first null equation now gives $R\eta=0$, and full column rank yields $\eta=0$. The augmented square matrix is injective and therefore nonsingular by finite-dimensional rank-nullity.

Nonsingularity gives a unique solution for every right-hand side. For the right-hand side $[f;0]$, multiply $Ku+R\gamma=f$ by $R^T$. Symmetry of $K$ and $KR=0$ imply $R^TK=0$, so $R^TR\gamma=R^Tf=0$ and positive definiteness gives $\gamma=0$. Hence $Ku=f$ and $R^Tu=0$. Conversely, any vector satisfying those two equations with multiplier zero solves the augmented system, so its uniqueness follows from step 3.1.

derivations.claim: Set $\eta(t)=\exp(-1/((t-1/4)(3/4-t)))$ for $1/4<t<3/4$ and $\eta(t)=0$ otherwise. At each endpoint every derivative from the interior is a finite sum of reciprocal-distance powers multiplied by $\exp(-c/\text{distance})$ for some $c>0$, hence tends to zero; so $\eta\in C_c^\infty(0,1)$. Put $\psi(x,y)=\eta(x)\eta(y)$ and $u=(\partial_y\psi,-\partial_x\psi)$. Equality of mixed derivatives gives $\operatorname{div}u=0$. Since $\eta(1/2)>0$ and $\eta(1/4)=0$, the mean value theorem gives $y\in(1/4,1/2)$ with $\eta'(y)>0$; hence $u_1(1/2,y)=\eta(1/2)\eta'(y)>0$. Thus $u\ne0$ and is compactly supported in $D$.

Let $f=-\operatorname{div}(2\varepsilon(u))\in C_c^\infty(D;\mathbb R^2)$. For $v\in C_c^\infty(D;\mathbb R^2)$, integration by parts and symmetry of $2\varepsilon(u)$ give $2(\varepsilon(u),\varepsilon(v))=(f,v)$. By [A1, F5], choose such tests converging to any given $v\in V$ in $H^1$; [F4] makes both pairings continuous under this convergence, so the identity holds for every $v\in V$.

A P1 vector field in this mesh vanishes at every boundary vertex and is determined by its center value $z=(a,b)$. On the bottom triangle the edge vectors from the center to its corners are $(-1/2,-1/2)$ and $(1/2,-1/2)$; its affine gradient $G$ maps both to $-z$. Subtracting gives the first column of $G$ zero, and adding gives the second column $(2a,2b)$, so divergence is $2b$. On the right triangle the edge vectors are $(1/2,-1/2)$ and $(1/2,1/2)$; subtraction gives the second column zero and addition the first column $(-2a,-2b)$, hence divergence is $-2a$. On the top triangle the edge vectors are $(1/2,1/2)$ and $(-1/2,1/2)$; subtraction gives the first column zero and addition the second column $(-2a,-2b)$, hence divergence is $-2b$. On the left triangle the edge vectors are $(-1/2,1/2)$ and $(-1/2,-1/2)$; subtraction gives the second column zero and addition the first column $(2a,2b)$, hence divergence is $2a$. If all four divergences vanish, then $a=b=0$, so the elementwise divergence-free subspace is exactly $\{0\}$.

Since $\operatorname{div}u=0$, the volumetric term vanishes and step 1.2 gives $\mathcal E_\lambda(u,v)=f(v)$ for every $v\in V$ and every finite $\lambda\ge0$. By [F1], this identifies the same nonzero $u$ as the unique continuous solution for each such $\lambda$.

The limit is zero by step 1.3. If the full family did not converge to zero, a sequence bounded away from zero would have such a zero-convergent subsequence, a contradiction.
